board-meeting-agenda.3: Use this board meeting agenda format for any US board. Add times; that keeps reports from crowding out decisions.
board-meeting-agenda.8: Number every item and state the decision needed. Then the secretary can write minutes straight into that structure, each agenda item becoming a minutes entry: a short summary, the motion, who moved and seconded, and the vote.
board-meeting-agenda.16: A consent agenda bundles routine, non-controversial items (approving minutes, committee reports, standard renewals) so the board approves them in one vote. Any director can ask to pull an item out for discussion.
board-meeting-agenda.18: Usually the board chair owns the agenda, preparing it with the CEO or executive director plus the secretary or governance staff, while committee chairs submit their items and directors can request topics through the chair.
board-meeting-agenda.21: Board minutes follow the agenda order. Per item, record the decision, motion, mover and seconder, and vote. Reusing your agenda as a minutes template saves time. Nothing gets missed.
board-meeting-agenda.24: The board chair sets the agenda, usually with the CEO or executive director and the board secretary. Directors can request items through the chair. Committee chairs submit their reports in advance, and the final version goes out with the packet so every director sees one identical plan.
board-meeting-agenda.25: Send the agenda and board packet 5 to 7 days before the meeting so directors can read reports and prepare questions. Quarterly board with long financial packs? 7 days is safer. Ask directors to send questions in advance, so meeting time goes to decisions rather than clarifications.
board-meeting-agenda.27: Old business covers items carried over from previous meetings; new business covers matters raised for the first time. Gradually, old business should shrink. Same item 3 meetings in a row without a decision? Give it a deadline or a smaller working group.
